Welcome toA Nudged Parcel

A blob of star gas is nudged upward in a layer hotter below: does it rise or return?

About: why a nudged parcel of gas inside a star swings back or keeps rising

About this simulation

On screen
Left: a slice through a model layer inside a Sun-like star, from 10 000 km below the height r to 30 000 km above it, the gas coloured by temperature on a fixed scale (deep orange at 2.25 × 106 K, pale yellow at 1.25 × 106 K). Dotted lines mark r and r + Δr. The Earth and a 10 000 km bar are drawn to the same scale. The 2 000 km parcel is tinted by its temperature relative to the gas beside it: brighter when hotter, darker and redder when cooler. After release, an arrow shows the buoyant force on it. Right: temperature against height above r, solid for the surrounding gas and dashed for the parcel as it is lifted, with dots at r + Δr.
Controls
The gradient |dT/dr| of the surrounding gas, 0 to 25 K/km, and the ratio of heat capacities γ (5/3, 1.4 or 1.2). Changing either returns the parcel to r at rest. Nudge ↑ lifts the parcel through Δr = 5 000 km in about one second and releases it; ⏮ Back to r returns it to r at rest.
Measured
t is the star's time in minutes since release; one second on screen is ten minutes in the star. z is the parcel's height above r. Tparcel is the parcel's own temperature, which exchanges no heat with the gas and keeps its pressure equal to the gas around it. Tgas is the surrounding gas at the same height. Both temperatures are in 106 K. Model: T0 = 2.0 × 106 K at r, pressure falling by e every 50 000 km, g = 500 m/s². The Readouts panel also gives Tparcel − Tgas, and, after the last question, the adiabatic gradient and whether the layer is stable.
Model
The parcel is the displaced “element” of the notes (§4.3). It cools at the adiabatic gradient |dT/dr|ad = (1 − 1/γ)T0/H, 16 K/km for γ = 5/3, and the layer is convective when the surrounding gas cools faster than that (the Schwarzschild criterion). This assumes a uniform composition: a gradient in the mean molecular weight, heavier gas below, can hold a layer stable (the Ledoux criterion). The parcel exchanges no heat and feels no drag, so a stable swing never dies away and an unstable parcel never mixes in. In zones where hydrogen is partly ionised the effective adiabatic exponent drops towards 1.2; the γ control stands for that effective value.

Guided Inquiry

1 · Lifting the parcel

Set γ = 5/3 and the temperature gradient of the surrounding gas to 10 K/km. The parcel will be lifted from r to r + Δr without exchanging heat with the gas around it. Before pressing Nudge, predict how its temperature at r + Δr compares with that of the gas around it there.

2 · Letting the parcel go

Keep the settings of question 1. The temperature of the layer falls outwards, hot gas below and cool gas above. Before pressing Nudge, predict what the parcel does after it is released.

3 · A layer at one temperature

Keep γ = 5/3 and set the temperature gradient of the surrounding gas to 0 K/km, so that the whole layer has the same temperature. Before pressing Nudge, predict how the swing compares with the one in question 2.

4 · A steeper gradient

Keep γ = 5/3 and set the temperature gradient of the surrounding gas to 25 K/km. Before pressing Nudge, predict what happens to the parcel.

5 · Sixteen kelvin per kilometre

Keep γ = 5/3 and set the temperature gradient of the surrounding gas to 16 K/km. Before pressing Nudge, predict what the parcel does after it is released.

6 · A lower gamma

Set the temperature gradient of the surrounding gas back to 10 K/km, which was stable in question 2, and change γ to 1.2. Before pressing Nudge, predict what happens.

7 · What you found

A displaced parcel cools at the adiabatic gradient |dT/dr|ad = (1 − 1/γ)T/H, 16 K/km here for γ = 5/3; the Readouts panel now shows it. If the gas around it cools more slowly with height, the parcel returns and swings about r: the layer is stable. If the gas cools faster, the parcel keeps rising: the layer convects. This is the Schwarzschild criterion. It assumes a uniform composition; heavier gas below can hold a layer stable (the Ledoux criterion).

01

At a glance

This sim lifts a parcel of gas by 5 000 km inside a Sun-like layer and lets it go. You change the layer and the gas to find what decides whether the parcel comes back.

What you'll learn

  • What happens to a parcel's temperature when it is carried up through a star.
  • How the temperature of the gas around it decides what the parcel does.
  • How the gas gradient and γ set which layers convect.
The setup: a parcel at r in a layer hot below and cool above, and the surrounding gas’s temperature against height.

What's on screen

  • The slice: gas coloured by temperature, from 10 000 km below r to 30 000 km above. Dotted lines mark r and r + Δr; the Earth gives the scale.
  • The parcel, 2 000 km across, tinted by its temperature against the gas beside it. After release an arrow shows the buoyant force.
  • Solid line: temperature of the surrounding gas against height. Dashed line: the parcel as it is lifted. Dots mark r + Δr.
  • Readouts: time, height, the two temperatures, their difference, and the verdict.
See itLook at the layer before any nudge. Watch for: the parcel sitting at r, with the solid temperature line falling as the height rises.

03

A lifted parcel cools as the pressure around it falls

The parcel moves slowly enough to keep the pressure of the gas around it, and fast enough to exchange no heat, so its change of state is adiabatic. For an ideal gas that gives T ∝ P(γ−1)/γ: as the pressure falls the parcel expands and cools. Differentiating gives the adiabatic temperature gradient, the notes’ (4.32):

Equation (4.32). It is the rate at which the temperature of the parcel falls as it rises.

Here the pressure falls by a factor e every 50 000 km, so (T/P)|dP/dr| = T0/H = 40 K/km. For γ = 5/3 the factor (1 − 1/γ) is 2/5, so the parcel cools at 16.0 K/km. Lifted 5 000 km, it loses 80 000 K and arrives at 1.920 × 106 K. The gas beside it, cooling at 10 K/km, is at 1.950 × 106 K.

Like the notes’ Figure 45(a), with the sim’s numbers: the parcel (dashed) ends cooler than the surroundings (solid).
Key idea. A lifted parcel follows its own adiabat, whatever the gas around it does.
See itPress Nudge with the opening settings: 10 K/km and γ = 5/3. Watch for: the dashed parcel line reaching 1.920 at the top of the lift, while the solid gas line passes 1.950 there. The readouts then keep following the parcel.
04

Cooler means denser, so it sinks: the Schwarzschild criterion

The parcel and the gas around it are at the same pressure. For gas of the same composition the density at a given pressure is inversely proportional to T. A parcel hotter than its surroundings is lighter and is pushed further up. A cooler one is denser and sinks back. Comparing the temperatures after the lift gives the Schwarzschild criterion, the notes’ (4.33):

Equation (4.33). The layer is unstable to convection if the gas cools with height faster than the adiabat. The left side is the gas gradient (the radiative gradient, in the notes).

At 10 K/km the gas cools less than the parcel, so the parcel arrives 30 000 K cooler and denser. It sinks, passes r, and is pushed back up from below. With no drag it swings for ever.

In the sim’s model the buoyant acceleration is g(Tparcel − Tgas)/T0, in proportion to the height z, and the swing has a period:

The sim’s model, not in the notes, for a stable layer. With g = 500 m/s² and T0 = 2.0 × 106 K, 10 K/km gives 86 min.
See itPress Nudge at 10 K/km and γ = 5/3, and watch for a whole swing. Watch for: the parcel dropping below r, rising back above it, and the height z reading going negative and then positive again, about every 86 min of star time.
05

The gas gradient moves the boundary between stable and convective

Keep γ = 5/3, so the parcel always arrives at 1.920 × 106 K, and change only the gas.

  • 0 K/km: the gas stays at 2.000 × 106 K and the parcel arrives 80 000 K cooler. The restoring force is stronger, and the period falls from 86 to 52 min.
  • 16 K/km: the gas and the parcel cool together. They have the same density at every height, so there is no buoyant force and the layer is neutral. This is the boundary of (4.33).
  • 25 K/km: the gas at r + Δr is 1.875 × 106 K, so the parcel is 45 000 K hotter and lighter. It keeps rising, faster and faster, and leaves the top of the slice after about 28 min.
The gas at r + Δr against the gas gradient. Left of 16 K/km the gas is hotter than the parcel; right of it, cooler.
|dT/dr| γ

These controls move the sim too. The numbers come from its own model.

See itSet the gradient to 0 K/km and press Nudge. Watch for: Tparcel − Tgas at the top of the lift, −80 000 K, before the parcel moves on and swings back with a period of 52 min.
See itSet the gradient to 16 K/km and press Nudge. Watch for: the dashed and solid lines meeting at r + Δr, the difference reading 0 K, and the parcel staying where it was put.
See itSet the gradient to 25 K/km and press Nudge. Watch for: the parcel hotter than the gas by 45 000 K at the top of the lift, then rising faster and faster out of the top of the slice.
06

A lower γ lowers the adiabat, so the same layer can convect

The adiabat depends on γ through the factor (1 − 1/γ), so for the same layer it is 16.0 K/km at γ = 5/3, 11.4 K/km at γ = 1.4 and 6.7 K/km at γ = 1.2.

The adiabatic gradient for the three values of γ. The dashed line is a gas gradient of 10 K/km.
  • γ = 1.4: the adiabat, 11.4 K/km, is still above 10 K/km. The parcel arrives 7 143 K cooler and swings back, slowly, with a period of 175 min.
  • γ = 1.2: the adiabat, 6.7 K/km, is below 10 K/km. The parcel arrives 16 667 K hotter and keeps rising: the layer convects.

In the layers where hydrogen is partly ionised, much of the energy added to the gas goes into ionising it, so γ is reduced (notes, 4.3). The γ control stands for that effective value.

See itKeep 10 K/km, choose γ = 1.4, and press Nudge. Watch for: a slow swing about r, with the layer reading stable, P = 175 min.
See itNow choose γ = 1.2 at the same 10 K/km and press Nudge. Watch for: the parcel hotter than the gas and rising, in the same layer that was stable at γ = 5/3.
07

Where it matters

  • Convective envelopes. The criterion is met where the radiative gradient is large: where the opacity is large, or the flux Lr/4πr2 is large, or γ is below 5/3 (notes, 4.3). The outer layers of a cool star meet it, since Kramers’ law makes the opacity rise as the temperature falls.
  • Partly ionised zones. There γ falls towards 1.2, which lowers the adiabat and can start convection in a layer that was stable.
  • The two stellar types. A star of about the Sun’s mass has a radiative interior and a convective envelope. A star several times more massive has a convective core and a radiative envelope (notes, Figure 46).

The derivation assumes the same mean molecular weight throughout. The sim also has no drag and no mixing, so a stable swing never dies away and an unstable parcel never mixes in.

08

Summary

In one line. A parcel of gas lifted inside a star either returns or keeps rising, and the layer’s gas gradient and γ decide which.

Key points

  • A lifted parcel cools at (1 − 1/γ)(T/P)|dP/dr|, 16.0 K/km here.
  • At the same pressure a cooler parcel is denser and sinks; a hotter one rises.
  • The layer convects when the gas cools with height faster than the adiabat.
  • A lower γ lowers the adiabat: 10 K/km is stable at 5/3, convective at 1.2.

Common mix-ups

  • "The parcel brings the deeper heat up, so it arrives hotter." It expands and cools, arriving at 1.920 × 106 K against the gas’s 1.950.
  • "No heat exchanged means the temperature stays at T0." Expanding, it does work and cools at 16.0 K/km.
  • "Hot gas below cool gas always turns over." Only if the gas cools faster than the parcel, and 10 K/km is slower than 16.0.

Things to try on your own

  • At γ = 5/3, step the gradient from 15 to 18 K/km: the swing slows, then gives way to a runaway.
  • At 10 K/km, step γ from 5/3 to 1.4 to 1.2 and compare the periods.
